name: homeworlds
desc: C++ framework for the game of Binary Homeworlds
why: Framework for Binary Homeworlds, a strange abstract two-player space game with a C++ engine you can play and extend.

brief.what_it_is: A C++ framework for Binary Homeworlds, a two-player strategy game played with Icehouse pieces in four colors and no board. The repository provides a C++14 core library (ApplyMove, AllMoves, InferMove, AIMove over GameState and WholeMove types), a command-line player and analyzer (homeworlds-cli), a wxWidgets graphical interface (homeworlds-wx), a Python extension (libhomeworlds), and a partial archive of SuperDuperGames.org game transcripts with a converter script. Input is a game state or moves typed or dragged on screen; output is legal move lists, applied states, and AI-chosen moves.
brief.why_it_exists: The author describes Homeworlds as "space chess" and builds a framework for working with the game, both to play against a computer and to experiment with analysis and AI. The README frames the project as a personal experiment and invites patches for a better GUI and a stronger AI.
brief.how_it_works: Pieces on the table represent star systems and spaceships, and the goal is to eliminate the enemy's homeworld ships by capture, catastrophe, or attacking the binary star system. The library represents states as GameState and moves as WholeMove, generates all legal moves, and can infer a full move from a partial entry such as "build g1". The GUI works by tracking mouse drags of pieces from the start position to the end position and deducing the move. The AI picks the best move from the full move list, and the README notes it cannot look far ahead because of the high branching factor.

commands_seen.context: Installs Python requirements for the libhomeworlds extension (one of two suggested install lines).
Installs the libhomeworlds Python module in editable mode from the v1.1.0 tag (the other suggested install line).
Runs the C++ unit tests; requires GTest to be installed first.
Special command typed at the homeworlds-cli prompt to have the computer make its move during a game against you.

brief.install_notes: No brew formula caveats. Building from source needs a C++14 compiler and make. The C++ unit tests need GTest installed separately, with a link to a Stack Overflow answer for instructions. The GUI needs wxWidgets. The Python module needs Python with setup.py and pip, and can be installed from the repository at tag v1.1.0. No accounts or hardware are needed; the game is normally played with Icehouse pieces but the software runs without them.
brief.standout: It is a small, open framework for an unusual abstract game whose core is a complete move generator, not just a rules checker. The GUI cleverly infers the intended move from a drag-and-drop board, and a SuperDuperGames transcript archive of over 700 games is bundled for analysis.
brief.status: Unknown from the README alone. The README references a v1.1.0 tag for the Python package, but it gives no release date, last commit date, or maintenance note, and I did not fetch the commit history or releases page. The README's tone ("poorly structured", "very weak" AI) suggests a hobby project, but it does not say it is abandoned.
brief.caveats: The README calls the C++ library "poorly structured" and says the internal representations are "fairly verbose and hard to manipulate (in terms of CPU cycles)". The author says the AI is "very weak" and cannot look more than one move ahead in practice. The GUI's visuals need work, according to the README. The Python install line uses a git:// URL, which many hosts no longer accept. The project is not affiliated with SuperDuperGames.org, BoardGameGeek, or Looney Labs. The GTest setup is left to an external link.
quotes: a two-player game of strategy and tactics that might aptly be described as "space chess"
This poorly structured library includes C++ data structures for SingleAction, WholeMove, PieceCollection, StarSystem, and GameState.
I know the current AI is very weak. The major hurdle is that it's not always feasible to look more than one move ahead, unless you can figure out how to prune bad moves.

judge.reason: Binary Homeworlds is an unusual boardless space-strategy game, and this framework makes its legal moves and game transcripts explorable rather than merely presenting another game client.

entry.title: Homeworlds
entry.tldr: A C++ framework, command-line player and GUI for Binary Homeworlds, a two-player "space chess" played with pyramids and no board.
entry.deeper_look:
Binary Homeworlds is an abstract strategy game for two players, normally played with Icehouse pieces in four colors. There is no board. Pieces on the table stand in for star systems and spaceships, and you win by eliminating the enemy's homeworld ships through capture, catastrophe, or attacking the binary star system. This project is a software framework for that game.

The core is a C++14 library with types such as GameState and WholeMove, and functions like ApplyMove, AllMoves, InferMove and AIMove. It is a full move generator, not only a rules checker. It can also infer a complete move from a partial entry such as "build g1". On top of the library sit homeworlds-cli, a command-line player and analyzer, and homeworlds-wx, a wxWidgets GUI that works out your move by tracking where you drag a piece from and to. There is also a Python extension and a partial archive of over 700 SuperDuperGames.org transcripts, with a converter script.

The author built it as a personal experiment, both to play against a computer and to explore analysis and AI. The README is frank about the state of things: the library is "poorly structured" and the AI is "very weak". The branching factor is high, so the AI cannot usually look more than one move ahead. That makes it an open problem rather than a finished product, and the README invites patches for a better GUI and a stronger AI.
entry.install:
brew install homeworlds
# pulls in wxwidgets for the GUI. No account or hardware needed; the Icehouse pieces are optional.

try_this.what_happens: Lists the options of the command-line player and analyzer.
Opens the graphical board, where you drag pieces and the program deduces the move.
Typed at the homeworlds-cli prompt during a game, it makes the computer play its move.

entry.whats_unique: It is a small, open framework around an unusual abstract game, built on a complete move generator. The GUI infers moves from drag and drop, and a bundled archive of real games is ready for analysis.
entry.caveats: The README calls the library poorly structured and the AI very weak, and it gives no maintenance status, so treat it as a hobby project.
